knowledgeDocuments.sampleSummary: The *Brahui Qaida* serves as a foundational pedagogical primer, outlining the basic structure of the Brahui alphabet, phonetic vowel-consonant combinations, and essential syllable-building rules. It organizes vocabulary into thematic clusters suitable for early learners, while emphasizing standardized orthography to preserve the language's distinct linguistic heritage across its varied dialects.

Lexicon (A-Z) 15-275 -- 4 of 276 -- 4 The English Brahui Dictionary It is our endeavor to preserve and promote the Brahui language, literature and Brahui cultural heritage, and popularize it to as many people as possible. Local people as well as non-locals have done valuable works on Brahui language. Among them, apart from Ge

rmans, Russians and Indians, British Orientalists also have a big contribution. However, the step-motherly treatment of the Brahui language by its own people is not a new thing, but it has been going on for the last Khans of Kalat. As this dictionary, by Duncan Dixey, was sent to Khan Kalat for publishing, after it was written, the Brahui Khan excused himself from printing and publishing it and returned it, saying that they had no money to print this precious work to preserve. Even after that, there have been repeated attempts by Balochistani politicians to eliminate this language under a certain deliberate plan. One such attempt was made by the NAP government in 1972. Not leaving a box for Brahui language in the 1998 census is another example of this kind. -- 5 of 276 -- 5 Thus Brahui has always been neglected by the politicians of Balochistan. It was not easy for the British to establish a foothold in the state of Kalat without learning the Brahui language, because in order to rule here, they had to learn the language so as to deal with its people. Hence the British Raj also fixed a scholarship for its scholars learning Brahui. In the early days when the Christian missionaries ca

me here to preach Christianity, the religious Brahuis Muslim tried to thwart their mission in their own way and chose their language as a medium to awaken the Brahui masses. Durkhani School was such an institute defending Islam directly and promoting Brahui indirectly. However, since the Brahui Academy has been established, the work of preserving the heritage of Brahui language and literature has built up. Due to Khan of Kalat's unwillingness to publish it, the dictionary was handed over to the British Museum for archiving, from where it was brought by Dr. Abdul Rahman Brahui and given to Brahui Academy for publishing. The dictionary was first published in 1995 by the Brahui Academy but at that time it was printed in the same script (common English script) as written by Duncan Dixey, so it was difficult -- 6 of 276 -- 6 for a non-Brahui, let alone a native Brahui to know the correct pronunciation of the words it contained. But before printing the second edition it was assigned to, Dr. Hafeezullah Sarparra to review the dictionary and rectify the mistakes of 1st edition, Dr. hafeezullah Sarparra, due to his linguistic friendliness for Brahui, has painstakingly composed it in phoneti

c Roman script as well as written Perso-Arabic (Nastalik) transliteration of the words in it, so as to pave the way for not only native Brahuis but also non-Brahui researchers and students to be benefited from it. Some revisions and additions have also been made to the dictionary, it is hoped that it will now be a useful work for the people having interest in Brahui language. Dr. M. Salah ud Din Mengal Chairman Brahui Academy (R) Pakistan, Quetta -- 7 of 276 -- 7 English- Brahui Dictionary By Rev: A. DUNCAN DIXEY Rev: DUNCAN Dixey was attached with Mission Hospital Quetta. Here he learnt Brahui and compiled an English to Brahui Dictionary in 1920. Next year in 1921 it was typed and in December 1923 a copy was gifted to British Museum London. One typed copy was in the library of Dr. R. Holland which he borrowed me and I myself typed three copies of it. After Independence 1947, a copy was sent to Government of Pakistan Karachi which was forwarded to N.W.F.P Frontier (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) for publication but it was returned as Brahui language was not spoken there. Then it was sent to Government of Balochistan, which was forwarded to Khan of Kalat. However, Kalat Government showed its i

nability to publish it and the typed manuscript was returned. During my stay in Britain in 1979, I had the opportunity to go through it again, on my return to Pakistan I handed over a typed copy to Brahui Academy Quetta. Due to paucity of funds it remained unpublished until 1994. I wanted to add a note about the original typed manuscript but without my consultation it was published as in those days, I was in Makran. For the information of readers, I give some facts about the original typed manuscript, which is spread over on 110 pages. The page No’s 99 and 100 are blank, and other facts are below: -- 8 of 276 -- 8 Words in English pages Nos No. of words A 1-5 261 B 6-12 314 C 13-20 399 D 21-25 259 E 26-29 151 F 30-34 275 G 34-37 262 H 37-42 94 I 42-45 102 J 45-46 42 K 46-47 42 L 47-51 189 M 51-55 256 N 55-57 97 O 57-59 78 P 59-65 237 Q 65-66 15 R 66-71 230 S 71-84 595 T 84-90 286 U 90-92 68 V 92 15 W 93-98 238 X --- --- Y 98 26 Z 98 3 By publishing this dictionary, it is now saved for generations to come. It is useful for those who are interested in Brahui language and literature. Dr. Abdul Rahman Brahui -- 9 of 276 -- 9 Preface (First Edition) Dictionary plays an important role in

the introduction and promotion of a language. In 1906 Mr. Duncan Dixey, started the work of compiling a Dictionary in Brahui language, but somehow the author could not complete and publish it. However, in 1921 it was completed and handed over to the Indian office library in the form of a manuscript, where it remained dumped for more than a half century. Dr. Abdul Rahman Brahui during his stay in England visited the said library and after weeks of strenuous search was able to unearth the manuscript. In spite of his own personal engagements he had to work hard for days in order to get a typed copy of the manuscript. Dr. Abdul Rahman Brahui was kind enough to accede to my request and handed over a copy of the same for my personal record. Mr. Salah Uddin Mengal took over the charge of the Chairmanship of the Brahui Academy in 1994 and under his dynamic leadership the matter of printing of the books was given special consideration. Taking advantage of this opportunity, I decided to -- 10 of 276 -- 10 make publish the unpresented work of Mr. Duncan Dixey in the form of a valuable Dictionary. After almost 75 years of laying foundations of this excellent job, I have the honor to present t

his great pioneering work of Mr. Duncan Dixey, in the form of a Dictionary, through the Brahui Academy. I sincerely hope that this book would render a great service to the people interested to gain knowledge about Brahui language. Prof. Aziz Mengal November 10th 1994. -- 11 of 276 -- 11 Preface (Reviewed Edition) Brahui is the oldest and the only Dravidian language of Pakistan. Henry Pottinger was first who introduced this language and its grammar to the West by his Travelogue “Travels in Sindh and Balochistan” in 1816. After that many writers and linguists analyzed and wrote on Brahui. During British rule over Kalat many English officers learnt and wrote on Brahui language, Duncan Dixey was also one of them, who during his job learnt Brahui here and started writing a dictionary in 1906 and after 15 years he succeeded to complete his book, but could not publish it then. About a half century after its completion this book was discovered by the pioneer of Brahui research Dr. Abdul Rahman Brahui and he handed over this unique work to Brahui academy for publishing. Its first edition was published in 1995, reviewed by Professor Aziz Mengal. Dictionary plays a vital role in preserving th

e cultural heritage of a language, I feel myself lucky and honored to be assigned the review of this important work done a century ago on Brahui language by a Non-Brahui. I have made some important revisions and additions in this book and tried to rectify the mistakes made in 1st edition also added the transliteration of words to make it easy to understand and well spell the Brahui words. -- 12 of 276 -- 12 No doubt, this precious lexical work of Brahui in English has much importance in the literary history of Brahui language. This book contains a number of borrowed words from Arabic and Persian languages which are commonly used in Brahui language, in spite of this, the Dictionary also preserves plentiful words of Brahui origin, some of which are archaic in Brahui language now. I am much thankful to the Brahui Academy specially the Chairman Dr. Salah ud Din Mengal for assigning me the important job of the review of this book to serve my mother tongue. I hope that the new and revised edition of this Dictionary would be much charitable for the students, scholars and teachers of Brahui language and also for the non-speakers to learn the lexicon of Brahui language. Dr. Hafeezullah Sarp

knowledgeDocuments.title: English to Brahui Dictionary
knowledgeDocuments.sampleSummary: This dictionary serves as a comprehensive lexicon documenting Brahui vocabulary through an English-to-Brahui translation framework, supplemented by a formal Romanization guide for Perso-Arabic scripts. While the primary focus is on lexical entries ranging from A to Z, the text functions as an academic resource that preserves the standard Brahui linguistic form through the collaborative editorial efforts of the Brahui Academy.

As the Brahui linguistic archivist, I have reviewed the *Brahui Qaida* provided. 

This foundational instructional text serves as a primary pedagogical tool, focusing on the Brahui alphabet, phonetic character combinations, and essential vocabulary through structured drills. It emphasizes standard linguistic patterns and orthographic conventions for beginning learners, though it maintains a focus on general acquisition rather than distinct regional dialectical variations.

As a Brahui linguistic archivist, I have summarized the provided text as follows:

This document formalizes Brahui's split-ergative alignment, specifically requiring subject pronouns to adopt an ergative marker when paired with transitive verbs in the past tense. chunks: ENGLISH-BRAHUI DICTIONARY -- 1 of 276 -- 1 Brahui Dictionary (English to Brahui) Albert Duncan Dixey Reviewed by: Dr. Hafeezullah Sarparra Brahui Academy (R) Pakistan, Quetta. -- 2 of 276 -- 2 (All Rights are reserved with Brahui Academy) Name of Book: Brahui Dictionary (English to Brahui) Author: Albert Duncan Dixey Review and additions: Dr. Hafeezullah Sarparra Supervised by: Dr. Salah ud Din Mengal Publisher: Brahui Academy (R) Pakistan, Quetta. Price: 600/- Year: 1921 1st Edition: 1995 2nd Edition: 2022 No. of Copies: 500 -- 3 of 276 -- 3 Content No. Content P. No 1. The English Brahui Dictionary Dr. Salah Uddin Mengal 04 2. English- Brahui Dictionary by Rev: A. DUNCAN DIXEY Dr. Abdul Rahman Brahui 07 3. Preface (1st Edition) Professor Aziz Mengal 09 4. Preface (2nd Edition) Dr. Hafeezullah Sarparra 11 5. Roman Transliteration of Perso-Arabic Letters 13 6. Lexicon (A-Z) 15-275 -- 4 of 276 -- 4 The English Brahui Dictionary It is our endeavor to preserve and promote the Brahui language, literature and Brahui cultural heritage, and popularize it to as many people as possible. Local people as well as non-locals have done valuable works on Brahui language. Among them, apart from Ge

rmans, Russians and Indians, British Orientalists also have a big contribution. However, the step-motherly treatment of the Brahui language by its own people is not a new thing, but it has been going on for the last Khans of Kalat. As this dictionary, by Duncan Dixey, was sent to Khan Kalat for publishing, after it was written, the Brahui Khan excused himself from printing and publishing it and returned it, saying that they had no money to print this precious work to preserve. Even after that, there have been repeated attempts by Balochistani politicians to eliminate this language under a certain deliberate plan. One such attempt was made by the NAP government in 1972. Not leaving a box for Brahui language in the 1998 census is another example of this kind. -- 5 of 276 -- 5 Thus Brahui has always been neglected by the politicians of Balochistan. It was not easy for the British to establish a foothold in the state of Kalat without learning the Brahui language, because in order to rule here, they had to learn the language so as to deal with its people. Hence the British Raj also fixed a scholarship for its scholars learning Brahui. In the early days when the Christian missionaries ca

me here to preach Christianity, the religious Brahuis Muslim tried to thwart their mission in their own way and chose their language as a medium to awaken the Brahui masses. Durkhani School was such an institute defending Islam directly and promoting Brahui indirectly. However, since the Brahui Academy has been established, the work of preserving the heritage of Brahui language and literature has built up. Due to Khan of Kalat's unwillingness to publish it, the dictionary was handed over to the British Museum for archiving, from where it was brought by Dr. Abdul Rahman Brahui and given to Brahui Academy for publishing. The dictionary was first published in 1995 by the Brahui Academy but at that time it was printed in the same script (common English script) as written by Duncan Dixey, so it was difficult -- 6 of 276 -- 6 for a non-Brahui, let alone a native Brahui to know the correct pronunciation of the words it contained. But before printing the second edition it was assigned to, Dr. Hafeezullah Sarparra to review the dictionary and rectify the mistakes of 1st edition, Dr. hafeezullah Sarparra, due to his linguistic friendliness for Brahui, has painstakingly composed it in phoneti

c Roman script as well as written Perso-Arabic (Nastalik) transliteration of the words in it, so as to pave the way for not only native Brahuis but also non-Brahui researchers and students to be benefited from it. Some revisions and additions have also been made to the dictionary, it is hoped that it will now be a useful work for the people having interest in Brahui language. Dr. M. Salah ud Din Mengal Chairman Brahui Academy (R) Pakistan, Quetta -- 7 of 276 -- 7 English- Brahui Dictionary By Rev: A. DUNCAN DIXEY Rev: DUNCAN Dixey was attached with Mission Hospital Quetta. Here he learnt Brahui and compiled an English to Brahui Dictionary in 1920. Next year in 1921 it was typed and in December 1923 a copy was gifted to British Museum London. One typed copy was in the library of Dr. R. Holland which he borrowed me and I myself typed three copies of it. After Independence 1947, a copy was sent to Government of Pakistan Karachi which was forwarded to N.W.F.P Frontier (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) for publication but it was returned as Brahui language was not spoken there. Then it was sent to Government of Balochistan, which was forwarded to Khan of Kalat. However, Kalat Government showed its i

nability to publish it and the typed manuscript was returned. During my stay in Britain in 1979, I had the opportunity to go through it again, on my return to Pakistan I handed over a typed copy to Brahui Academy Quetta. Due to paucity of funds it remained unpublished until 1994. I wanted to add a note about the original typed manuscript but without my consultation it was published as in those days, I was in Makran. For the information of readers, I give some facts about the original typed manuscript, which is spread over on 110 pages. The page No’s 99 and 100 are blank, and other facts are below: -- 8 of 276 -- 8 Words in English pages Nos No. of words A 1-5 261 B 6-12 314 C 13-20 399 D 21-25 259 E 26-29 151 F 30-34 275 G 34-37 262 H 37-42 94 I 42-45 102 J 45-46 42 K 46-47 42 L 47-51 189 M 51-55 256 N 55-57 97 O 57-59 78 P 59-65 237 Q 65-66 15 R 66-71 230 S 71-84 595 T 84-90 286 U 90-92 68 V 92 15 W 93-98 238 X --- --- Y 98 26 Z 98 3 By publishing this dictionary, it is now saved for generations to come. It is useful for those who are interested in Brahui language and literature. Dr. Abdul Rahman Brahui -- 9 of 276 -- 9 Preface (First Edition) Dictionary plays an important role in

the introduction and promotion of a language. In 1906 Mr. Duncan Dixey, started the work of compiling a Dictionary in Brahui language, but somehow the author could not complete and publish it. However, in 1921 it was completed and handed over to the Indian office library in the form of a manuscript, where it remained dumped for more than a half century. Dr. Abdul Rahman Brahui during his stay in England visited the said library and after weeks of strenuous search was able to unearth the manuscript. In spite of his own personal engagements he had to work hard for days in order to get a typed copy of the manuscript. Dr. Abdul Rahman Brahui was kind enough to accede to my request and handed over a copy of the same for my personal record. Mr. Salah Uddin Mengal took over the charge of the Chairmanship of the Brahui Academy in 1994 and under his dynamic leadership the matter of printing of the books was given special consideration. Taking advantage of this opportunity, I decided to -- 10 of 276 -- 10 make publish the unpresented work of Mr. Duncan Dixey in the form of a valuable Dictionary. After almost 75 years of laying foundations of this excellent job, I have the honor to present t

his great pioneering work of Mr. Duncan Dixey, in the form of a Dictionary, through the Brahui Academy. I sincerely hope that this book would render a great service to the people interested to gain knowledge about Brahui language. Prof. Aziz Mengal November 10th 1994. -- 11 of 276 -- 11 Preface (Reviewed Edition) Brahui is the oldest and the only Dravidian language of Pakistan. Henry Pottinger was first who introduced this language and its grammar to the West by his Travelogue “Travels in Sindh and Balochistan” in 1816. After that many writers and linguists analyzed and wrote on Brahui. During British rule over Kalat many English officers learnt and wrote on Brahui language, Duncan Dixey was also one of them, who during his job learnt Brahui here and started writing a dictionary in 1906 and after 15 years he succeeded to complete his book, but could not publish it then. About a half century after its completion this book was discovered by the pioneer of Brahui research Dr. Abdul Rahman Brahui and he handed over this unique work to Brahui academy for publishing. Its first edition was published in 1995, reviewed by Professor Aziz Mengal. Dictionary plays a vital role in preserving th

e cultural heritage of a language, I feel myself lucky and honored to be assigned the review of this important work done a century ago on Brahui language by a Non-Brahui. I have made some important revisions and additions in this book and tried to rectify the mistakes made in 1st edition also added the transliteration of words to make it easy to understand and well spell the Brahui words. -- 12 of 276 -- 12 No doubt, this precious lexical work of Brahui in English has much importance in the literary history of Brahui language. This book contains a number of borrowed words from Arabic and Persian languages which are commonly used in Brahui language, in spite of this, the Dictionary also preserves plentiful words of Brahui origin, some of which are archaic in Brahui language now. I am much thankful to the Brahui Academy specially the Chairman Dr. Salah ud Din Mengal for assigning me the important job of the review of this book to serve my mother tongue. I hope that the new and revised edition of this Dictionary would be much charitable for the students, scholars and teachers of Brahui language and also for the non-speakers to learn the lexicon of Brahui language. Dr. Hafeezullah Sarp

knowledgeDocuments.sampleSummary: This dictionary serves as a comprehensive lexicon facilitating English-to-Brahui translation, organized alphabetically from A to Z with standardized Roman transliterations of Perso-Arabic characters. While primarily focused on vocabulary acquisition, it functions as a scholarly preservation effort by the Brahui Academy, incorporating both historical 1921 source material and modern lexicographical revisions.

Lexicon (A-Z) 15-275 -- 4 of 276 -- 4 The English Brahui Dictionary It is our endeavor to preserve and promote the Brahui language, literature and Brahui cultural heritage, and popularize it to as many people as possible. Local people as well as non-locals have done valuable works on Brahui language. Among them, apart from Ge

rmans, Russians and Indians, British Orientalists also have a big contribution. However, the step-motherly treatment of the Brahui language by its own people is not a new thing, but it has been going on for the last Khans of Kalat. As this dictionary, by Duncan Dixey, was sent to Khan Kalat for publishing, after it was written, the Brahui Khan excused himself from printing and publishing it and returned it, saying that they had no money to print this precious work to preserve. Even after that, there have been repeated attempts by Balochistani politicians to eliminate this language under a certain deliberate plan. One such attempt was made by the NAP government in 1972. Not leaving a box for Brahui language in the 1998 census is another example of this kind. -- 5 of 276 -- 5 Thus Brahui has always been neglected by the politicians of Balochistan. It was not easy for the British to establish a foothold in the state of Kalat without learning the Brahui language, because in order to rule here, they had to learn the language so as to deal with its people. Hence the British Raj also fixed a scholarship for its scholars learning Brahui. In the early days when the Christian missionaries ca

me here to preach Christianity, the religious Brahuis Muslim tried to thwart their mission in their own way and chose their language as a medium to awaken the Brahui masses. Durkhani School was such an institute defending Islam directly and promoting Brahui indirectly. However, since the Brahui Academy has been established, the work of preserving the heritage of Brahui language and literature has built up. Due to Khan of Kalat's unwillingness to publish it, the dictionary was handed over to the British Museum for archiving, from where it was brought by Dr. Abdul Rahman Brahui and given to Brahui Academy for publishing. The dictionary was first published in 1995 by the Brahui Academy but at that time it was printed in the same script (common English script) as written by Duncan Dixey, so it was difficult -- 6 of 276 -- 6 for a non-Brahui, let alone a native Brahui to know the correct pronunciation of the words it contained. But before printing the second edition it was assigned to, Dr. Hafeezullah Sarparra to review the dictionary and rectify the mistakes of 1st edition, Dr. hafeezullah Sarparra, due to his linguistic friendliness for Brahui, has painstakingly composed it in phoneti

c Roman script as well as written Perso-Arabic (Nastalik) transliteration of the words in it, so as to pave the way for not only native Brahuis but also non-Brahui researchers and students to be benefited from it. Some revisions and additions have also been made to the dictionary, it is hoped that it will now be a useful work for the people having interest in Brahui language. Dr. M. Prof. Aziz Mengal November 10th 1994. -- 11 of 276 -- 11 Preface (Reviewed Edition) Brahui is the oldest and the only Dravidian language of Pakistan. Henry Pottinger was first who introduced this language and its grammar to the West by his Travelogue “Travels in Sindh and Balochistan” in 1816. After that many writers and linguists analyzed and wrote on Brahui. During British rule over Kalat many English officers learnt and wrote on Brahui language, Duncan Dixey was also one of them, who during his job learnt Brahui here and started writing a dictionary in 1906 and after 15 years he succeeded to complete his book, but could not publish it then. About a half century after its completion this book was discovered by the pioneer of Brahui research Dr. Abdul Rahman Brahui and he handed over this unique work to Brahui academy for publishing. Its first edition was published in 1995, reviewed by Professor Aziz Mengal. Dictionary plays a vital role in preserving th

e cultural heritage of a language, I feel myself lucky and honored to be assigned the review of this important work done a century ago on Brahui language by a Non-Brahui. I have made some important revisions and additions in this book and tried to rectify the mistakes made in 1st edition also added the transliteration of words to make it easy to understand and well spell the Brahui words. -- 12 of 276 -- 12 No doubt, this precious lexical work of Brahui in English has much importance in the literary history of Brahui language. This book contains a number of borrowed words from Arabic and Persian languages which are commonly used in Brahui language, in spite of this, the Dictionary also preserves plentiful words of Brahui origin, some of which are archaic in Brahui language now. I am much thankful to the Brahui Academy specially the Chairman Dr. Salah ud Din Mengal for assigning me the important job of the review of this book to serve my mother tongue. I hope that the new and revised edition of this Dictionary would be much charitable for the students, scholars and teachers of Brahui language and also for the non-speakers to learn the lexicon of Brahui language. Lexicon (A-Z) 15-275 -- 4 of 276 -- 4 The English Brahui Dictionary It is our endeavor to preserve and promote the Brahui language, literature and Brahui cultural heritage, and popularize it to as many people as possible. Local people as well as non-locals have done valuable works on Brahui language. Among them, apart from Ge

rmans, Russians and Indians, British Orientalists also have a big contribution. However, the step-motherly treatment of the Brahui language by its own people is not a new thing, but it has been going on for the last Khans of Kalat. As this dictionary, by Duncan Dixey, was sent to Khan Kalat for publishing, after it was written, the Brahui Khan excused himself from printing and publishing it and returned it, saying that they had no money to print this precious work to preserve. Even after that, there have been repeated attempts by Balochistani politicians to eliminate this language under a certain deliberate plan. One such attempt was made by the NAP government in 1972. Not leaving a box for Brahui language in the 1998 census is another example of this kind. -- 5 of 276 -- 5 Thus Brahui has always been neglected by the politicians of Balochistan. It was not easy for the British to establish a foothold in the state of Kalat without learning the Brahui language, because in order to rule here, they had to learn the language so as to deal with its people. Hence the British Raj also fixed a scholarship for its scholars learning Brahui. In the early days when the Christian missionaries ca

me here to preach Christianity, the religious Brahuis Muslim tried to thwart their mission in their own way and chose their language as a medium to awaken the Brahui masses. Durkhani School was such an institute defending Islam directly and promoting Brahui indirectly. However, since the Brahui Academy has been established, the work of preserving the heritage of Brahui language and literature has built up. Due to Khan of Kalat's unwillingness to publish it, the dictionary was handed over to the British Museum for archiving, from where it was brought by Dr. Abdul Rahman Brahui and given to Brahui Academy for publishing. The dictionary was first published in 1995 by the Brahui Academy but at that time it was printed in the same script (common English script) as written by Duncan Dixey, so it was difficult -- 6 of 276 -- 6 for a non-Brahui, let alone a native Brahui to know the correct pronunciation of the words it contained. But before printing the second edition it was assigned to, Dr. Hafeezullah Sarparra to review the dictionary and rectify the mistakes of 1st edition, Dr. hafeezullah Sarparra, due to his linguistic friendliness for Brahui, has painstakingly composed it in phoneti

c Roman script as well as written Perso-Arabic (Nastalik) transliteration of the words in it, so as to pave the way for not only native Brahuis but also non-Brahui researchers and students to be benefited from it. Some revisions and additions have also been made to the dictionary, it is hoped that it will now be a useful work for the people having interest in Brahui language. Dr. M. Salah ud Din Mengal Chairman Brahui Academy (R) Pakistan, Quetta -- 7 of 276 -- 7 English- Brahui Dictionary By Rev: A. DUNCAN DIXEY Rev: DUNCAN Dixey was attached with Mission Hospital Quetta. Here he learnt Brahui and compiled an English to Brahui Dictionary in 1920. Next year in 1921 it was typed and in December 1923 a copy was gifted to British Museum London. One typed copy was in the library of Dr. R. Holland which he borrowed me and I myself typed three copies of it. After Independence 1947, a copy was sent to Government of Pakistan Karachi which was forwarded to N.W.F.P Frontier (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) for publication but it was returned as Brahui language was not spoken there. Then it was sent to Government of Balochistan, which was forwarded to Khan of Kalat. However, Kalat Government showed its i

nability to publish it and the typed manuscript was returned. During my stay in Britain in 1979, I had the opportunity to go through it again, on my return to Pakistan I handed over a typed copy to Brahui Academy Quetta. Due to paucity of funds it remained unpublished until 1994. I wanted to add a note about the original typed manuscript but without my consultation it was published as in those days, I was in Makran. For the information of readers, I give some facts about the original typed manuscript, which is spread over on 110 pages. the introduction and promotion of a language. In 1906 Mr. Duncan Dixey, started the work of compiling a Dictionary in Brahui language, but somehow the author could not complete and publish it. However, in 1921 it was completed and handed over to the Indian office library in the form of a manuscript, where it remained dumped for more than a half century. Dr. Abdul Rahman Brahui during his stay in England visited the said library and after weeks of strenuous search was able to unearth the manuscript. In spite of his own personal engagements he had to work hard for days in order to get a typed copy of the manuscript. Dr. Abdul Rahman Brahui was kind enough to accede to my request and handed over a copy of the same for my personal record. Mr. Salah Uddin Mengal took over the charge of the Chairmanship of the Brahui Academy in 1994 and under his dynamic leadership the matter of printing of the books was given special consideration. Taking advantage of this opportunity, I decided to -- 10 of 276 -- 10 make publish the unpresented work of Mr. Duncan Dixey in the form of a valuable Dictionary. After almost 75 years of laying foundations of this excellent job, I have the honor to present t

his great pioneering work of Mr. Duncan Dixey, in the form of a Dictionary, through the Brahui Academy. I sincerely hope that this book would render a great service to the people interested to gain knowledge about Brahui language. Prof. Aziz Mengal November 10th 1994. -- 11 of 276 -- 11 Preface (Reviewed Edition) Brahui is the oldest and the only Dravidian language of Pakistan. Henry Pottinger was first who introduced this language and its grammar to the West by his Travelogue “Travels in Sindh and Balochistan” in 1816. After that many writers and linguists analyzed and wrote on Brahui. During British rule over Kalat many English officers learnt and wrote on Brahui language, Duncan Dixey was also one of them, who during his job learnt Brahui here and started writing a dictionary in 1906 and after 15 years he succeeded to complete his book, but could not publish it then. About a half century after its completion this book was discovered by the pioneer of Brahui research Dr. Abdul Rahman Brahui and he handed over this unique work to Brahui academy for publishing. Its first edition was published in 1995, reviewed by Professor Aziz Mengal. Dictionary plays a vital role in preserving th

e cultural heritage of a language, I feel myself lucky and honored to be assigned the review of this important work done a century ago on Brahui language by a Non-Brahui. I have made some important revisions and additions in this book and tried to rectify the mistakes made in 1st edition also added the transliteration of words to make it easy to understand and well spell the Brahui words. -- 12 of 276 -- 12 No doubt, this precious lexical work of Brahui in English has much importance in the literary history of Brahui language. This book contains a number of borrowed words from Arabic and Persian languages which are commonly used in Brahui language, in spite of this, the Dictionary also preserves plentiful words of Brahui origin, some of which are archaic in Brahui language now. I am much thankful to the Brahui Academy specially the Chairman Dr. Salah ud Din Mengal for assigning me the important job of the review of this book to serve my mother tongue. I hope that the new and revised edition of this Dictionary would be much charitable for the students, scholars and teachers of Brahui language and also for the non-speakers to learn the lexicon of Brahui language. Dr. Hafeezullah Sarp

knowledgeDocuments.sampleSummary: This comprehensive dictionary serves as a repository of Brahui vocabulary, documenting extensive lexical entries from A to Z alongside a structured guide for the Roman transliteration of Perso-Arabic scripts. While the text primarily functions as a foundational English-to-Brahui lexicon, it acts as a significant archival effort by the Brahui Academy to standardize linguistic preservation across contemporary dialects.

chunks: 1. Brahui SOV Structure: - Always reorder the output sentence into: [Subject] + [Object / Complement] + [Verb]. - Example: "He abducts" -> "O narrifik" (Subject + Verb) - Example: "He accepts advice" -> "O pant e mannik" (Subject + Object + Verb) 2. Action Verbs ending in "kanning" (To do / make): - Verbs formed with "kanning" (e.g., Abate -> "Ççiṭ manning", Abstain -> "Parhēz kanning", Accomplish -> "Purā kanning", Accompany -> "Awar hining") must maintain the auxiliary verb at the absolute end of the clause. 3. Compound Verbs & Adjectives: - For adjectives like "Afraid" -> "Xulōk / Xulīng", place the emotion word before the auxiliary state verb ("manning" / "manning"). 4. Punctuation Strip Rule: - Pre-process any input text by stripping trailing periods (.) or punctuation before matching dictionary lookups, then re-apply proper sentence-ending markers post-translation. 5. Prepositions to Postpositions Transition: - English prepositions like "About" (Bābat aṭ), "Above" (Burza / Katumāē), "Across" (Dāpār ēpār), "Amid" (Niāmaṭī) must be attached or placed AFTER the noun in Brahui (Postpositional Logic).

### Rule 1: Strict Clause-Final Verb Word Order (SOV) [From: Brahui SOV]
Category: Syntax

### Rule 1: Strict Clause-Final SOV Word Order
Category: Syntax
Pattern: [Subject] + [Object / Complement] + [Verb]
Explanation: Brahui strictly follows a Subject-Object-Verb (SOV) word order structure, requiring objects, complements, and verbal elements to precede the main verb or auxiliary at the end of the clause.
Example (Correct): O pant e mannik
Example (Incorrect): O mannik pant e
Gloss: He accepts advice

---

### Rule 2: Auxiliary Final Positioning in Compound Verbs
Category: Morphology
Pattern: [Noun/Adjective Stem] + [Auxiliary Verb: kanning / manning]
Explanation: Verbs formed with light or auxiliary verbs such as 'kanning' (to do/make) or 'manning' (to become) must position the auxiliary element at the absolute end of the clause, following the nominal or adjectival root.
Example (Correct): Parhēz kanning
Example (Incorrect): kanning parhēz
Gloss: To abstain

---

### Rule 3: Preposition-to-Postposition Inversion
Category: Syntax
Pattern: [Noun] + [Postposition / Case Suffix]
Explanation: Unlike English which uses prepositions, Brahui employs postpositions. Adpositions and locative/relational markers must be placed after the noun they govern (Postpositional Logic).
Example (Correct): Bābat aṭ
Example (Incorrect): aṭ bābat
Gloss: About

### Rule 4: Adjectival Predicate State Order
Category: Syntax
Pattern: [Emotion / Adjective Stem] + [State Auxiliary: manning]
Explanation: Compound adjectives and emotional states (such as 'Xulōk' meaning afraid) precede their state-marking auxiliary verb ('manning') within the phrasal structure.
Example (Correct): Xulōk manning
Example (Incorrect): manning xulōk

chunks: Brahui Grammar Part I: Noun Declension. Nominative case has no suffix. Genitive affix is -na. Dative suffix is -e. Locative affixes are -āī (upon) and -ṭī (in, inside). Ablative is -ān (from). Associative suffix is -to (with). Purposive suffix is -ki (for).
Verbal Conjugation: Present-Future tense suffixes for Person: 1st Sing: -va/ -uţ; 2nd Sing: -sa / -us; 3rd Sing: -ik / -e; 1st Plur: -ona / -un; 2nd Plur: -ere / -ure; 3rd Plur: -ira / -o.

Negative conjugation: Formed by infusing -pa- or -fa- infix between the root and verbal inflectional termination. Example: karing (to do) -> kappara (I do not do), kunēk (he eats) -> kumpak (he does not eat).

Between your fingers you hold a stone and throw it into flowing water. The effect might not be easy to see. There will be a small ripple where the stone breaks the surface and then a splash, muffled by the rush of the surrounding river. That’s all.

Chapter 1: The Land of Balochistan.

Brahui is an ancient language spoken in Kalat and across the mountain valleys. The people have preserved their culture and language for generations.

Today, scholars and linguists study its Dravidian roots and unique grammar.
translationLogs.translatedText:
باب 1: بلوچستان نا متم.

براہوئی اسہ قدیم آ بولی اس ءِ ہرا قلات او غرتا نا وادی تی ٹی ہیت مریک. الس تینا کلچر او بولی ءِ نسل در نسل بچین ءِ.

مرو، ماہرین علم او لسانیات اسہ ڈراوڑی ریشہ او تینا گونا اٹی ہیت کننگ تیا تحقیق کیر۔

Chapter 1: The Land of Balochistan.

Brahui is an ancient language spoken in Kalat and across the mountain valleys. The people have preserved their culture and language for generations.

Today, scholars and linguists study its Dravidian roots and unique grammar.
translationLogs.translatedText:
اولیکو بشخ: بلوچستان نا ڈغار۔

براہوئی اسہ مستین ءُ زبان اس ءِ ہرا قلات او مش نا درہ غاتیٹی ہیت کننگک۔ بندغاک پڑیا تیان تینا دود و ربیدگ او زبان ءِ سنبھال کرینو۔

اینو، عالم آک او لسانیات دان آک اینا دراوڑی بنیاد او بے مٹ گرائمر نا پٹ و پول ءِ کیرہ۔

translationLogs.sourceText: Brahui is a unique language spoken predominantly in Balochistan. Unlike its neighboring Indo-Aryan and Iranian languages, Brahui is historically classified as a Northern Dravidian language. Scholars continue to study its rich oral traditions and distinct grammatical features.
translationLogs.translatedText: براہوئی اسہ بے مٹ ءُ زبان اس ءِ ہرا گیشتر بلوچستان ٹی ہیت کننگک۔ تینا ہمسایہ انڈو آرین او ایرانی زبان تیان جتا، براہوئی تواریخی وڑاٹ اسہ قطبی دراوڑی زبان اس گوندنگک۔ زانتکار آک اونا گنجین زبانی روایت او جتا ءُ قواعدی صفت آتا مطالعہ ءِ برجا تخانو۔
